extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and litigants in TTAB inter partes proceedings (trademark/IP attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and practical guidance for taking, noticing, objecting to, certifying, and using discovery depositions (including depositions on written questions) and interrogatories in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board inter partes proceedings. Covers timing, form, service, objections, and differences from testimony depositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions on written questions — before whom taken
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition upon written questions may be taken before any person before whom depositions may be taken as provided by Rule 28 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (37 CFR § 2.124(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat depositions on written questions the same as depositions on oral examination for purposes of who may preside. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 28 and TBMP § 404.04 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions on written questions — timing (when taken)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be both noticed and taken during the discovery period (37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiate the procedure early in the discovery period. Whether to suspend unrelated discovery activities while a written-questions deposition is pending is within the Board’s scheduling discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions on written questions — place of deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Place of a discovery deposition on written questions is governed by TBMP § 404.03 and relevant CFR provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult TBMP § 404.03 for specifics about where to take the deposition; the TBMP cross-references control location rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of deposition on written questions — contents and filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A party desiring to take a discovery deposition on written questions shall serve notice upon each adverse party and file a copy of the notice (but not copies of the questions) with the Board; notice must state the name and address (if known) of the person to be deposed or a sufficient descriptive identification if name unknown (37 CFR § 2.124(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If name unknown, provide a descriptive class so the responding party can designate appropriate persons (Rule 30(b)(6)-type designation). The notice filed with the Board should be accompanied by the name or descriptive title of the officer before whom the deposition will be taken (37 CFR § 2.124(c)). Copies of notices served on adverse parties must be accompanied by the written questions (37 CFR § 2.124(d)(1)). See TBMP § 404.05 for general deposition-notice guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure and timelines for written-questions depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Timetables for service: within 20 days (25 if mailed) after notice, adverse parties may serve cross questions; within 10 days (15 if mailed) deposing party may serve redirect; within 10 days (15 if mailed) cross may serve recross; objections and substitute questions have corresponding 10/15-day periods (37 CFR § 2.124(d)(1)–(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may extend any of these periods for good cause or on its own initiative (37 CFR § 2.124(d)(2)). After the last date for questions/objections/substitute questions, the deposing party must mail the notice and all questions to the designated officer; the officer records each answer immediately after the corresponding question and certifies the transcript (37 CFR § 2.124(e)). See statutory day-count adjustments for service by mail/overnight courier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections in written-questions depositions — form and preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Written objections to questions may be served and must be served on every other adverse party; substitute questions may be served in response to objections within the prescribed period. Objections to questions and answers may be considered at final hearing (37 CFR § 2.124(d)(1) & (g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If revised questions overcome objections, the objecting party should file notice identifying objections no longer at issue. Objections not maintained in a brief at final hearing may be deemed waived. See TBMP § 703.02(k) and TBMP §§ 707.03(c), 707.04 for preservation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and signature of depositions on written questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The officer designated shall record each answer immediately after the corresponding question and shall certify the transcript (37 CFR § 2.124(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For form specifics and signature requirements in inter partes proceedings, see 37 CFR § 2.123(g) and TBMP § 703.01(i); for signature rules see 37 CFR § 2.123(e)(5) and TBMP § 703.01(j). Ensure correct form before certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification, service, and correction of written-question deposition transcripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Within ten days after the last date for questions/objections/substitute questions, the deposing party mails the notice and all questions to the officer; the officer certifies and mails the transcript and exhibits to the deposing party; the party that took the deposition must promptly serve the transcript and exhibits on every adverse party and assure the transcript is correct (37 CFR § 2.124(e)–(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deposition is to be made of record, follow 37 CFR § 2.120(j) procedures and TBMP § 704.09. For correcting errors in testimony depositions see TBMP § 703.01(n) and 37 CFR § 2.125(b). See cited cases (e.g., Fischer Gesellschaft) for precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of depositions on written questions — pros and cons
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions on written questions are cumbersome and time-consuming, deprive parties of face-to-face confrontation and follow-up questioning, but may be the only feasible means for foreign depositions and may be less expensive and more convenient for witnesses (37 CFR § 2.124 commentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the trade-offs: use written-questions depositions when oral examination is infeasible (e.g., foreign witness), but be aware of limitations on probing and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of objections to discovery depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to the taking of a discovery deposition may include errors/irregularities in the notice, manner of taking, form of question/answer, oath/affirmation, party conduct, disqualification of officer, witness competency, or competency/relevancy/materiality of testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objections derive from Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(c)(2), 32(d)(1)–(3). Distinguish objections that must be made promptly (or are waived) from those that can be preserved for hearing (e.g., competency/relevancy may be preserved if ground could not have been corrected at the time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to notice of deposition — timing and waiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to errors or irregularities in a deposition notice must be promptly served in writing on the party giving the notice; failure to serve such objections promptly results in waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare case law on facial sufficiency of notices and when objections are timely (e.g., Sunrider Corp. v. Raats, Steiger Tractor, etc.). For motions to quash or protective orders see TBMP §§ 521 and 410.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections as to disqualification of the officer — timing
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection to taking a discovery deposition because of disqualification of the officer is waived unless made before the deposition begins or as soon thereafter as the disqualification becomes known or could have been discovered with reasonable diligence (Fed. R. Civ. P. 32(d)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise officer-disqualification objections immediately upon discovery; otherwise waiver applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections during deposition — concise, nonargumentative, and limits on instructing not to answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections during depositions must be stated concisely and nonargumentatively; a person may instruct a deponent not to answer only to preserve a privilege, to enforce a limitation ordered by the court/Board, or to present a motion under Rule 30(d)(3) (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(c)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, objections should be limited to grounds that might be waived if not made at the deposition. Questions objected to should ordinarily be answered subject to the objection unless privileged or protected by an approved protective order. See TBMP § 404.07(f) for written-questions specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver rules for objections to errors/irregularities at oral discovery depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection to an error or irregularity relating to manner of taking deposition, form of question/answer, oath, conduct, or other correctable matters is waived if not made seasonably during the deposition (Fed. R. Civ. P. 32(d)(3)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a ground for objection could have been corrected at the deposition, failing to object then generally results in waiver; maintain objections in final briefs to avoid waiver at hearing (see cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences when a witness refuses to answer at a deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If a witness refuses to answer particular questions, the propounding party may seek subpoena or court order (for testimonial depositions) or, for discovery depositions, complete the deposition and file a motion to compel with the Board (where applicable). If at final hearing the Board finds the refusal unjustified, it may presume the answer would have been unfavorable or reduce the testimony's probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For testimony depositions there is no motion to compel available before final hearing — the propounding party may need to apply to the district court under 35 U.S.C. § 24 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 45. See TBMP § 411.04 and cited authorities (e.g., Ferro Corp., Health-Tex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery depositions vs testimony depositions — purpose and scope differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions are broad devices to obtain information about an adversary’s case (may seek information not admissible at trial if reasonably calculated to lead to admissible evidence); testimony depositions are narrower, used to present evidence and limited to evidence admissible under applicable rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that discovery depositions occur during the joint discovery period; testimony depositions occur only during a party's assigned testimony period. Inadmissibility may be a ground for objection in testimonial depositions. See TBMP § 404.09 and governing CFR and FRCP citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery vs testimony depositions — timing, filing, and making part of record
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be taken during discovery period and do not become part of evidentiary record unless offered via notice of reliance during a party’s testimony period; testimony depositions must be filed when taken and become part of the record without a notice of reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To offer a discovery deposition into evidence, follow 37 CFR § 2.120(j) and TBMP § 704.09. Testimony depositions of adverse parties generally require a subpoena if not voluntary (see 35 U.S.C. § 24 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 30/45).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery depositions — remedies and strategic considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For discovery depositions, the propounding party has the option of completing the deposition and later filing a motion to compel; for testimony depositions, immediate court action may be required if a witness refuses to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the simpler alternative of completing discovery depositions and seeking Board relief post-deposition. Beware that refusal to answer in testimony depositions can be deemed adverse at final hearing; plan subpoenas and timing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatories — when permitted and who may serve them
rubrics_metrics.description: For inter partes proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, written interrogatories may be served on another party during the discovery period only if the serving party previously or concurrently served its initial disclosures, absent stipulation, motion, or Board order. Interrogatories may not be served on non-parties (37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3), Fed. R. Civ. P. 33).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrogatories may be served from the opening of the discovery period through its last day; answers to later-served interrogatories may be served after the discovery period closes. Consult TBMP § 403.01 and § 403.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatories — scope and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogatories may seek any information discoverable under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b); an otherwise proper interrogatory is not objectionable merely because it requires an opinion or contention applying law to fact (Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases hold parties may be required to answer interrogatories asking for legal conclusions about the case (e.g., whether marks are confusingly similar). Frame contention/interrogatory questions carefully given disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatories — numeric limit and motion for additional interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Total number of written interrogatories served on another party in a proceeding shall not exceed seventy-five, counting subparts, unless the Board allows additional interrogatories on motion showing good cause or by stipulation (37 CFR § 2.120(d)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion for leave to serve additional interrogatories must be filed and granted before serving extra interrogatories and must include copies of already-served and proposed interrogatories. Good-cause standard is applied narrowly (case law indicates legitimate need must be shown). Parties may stipulate to a lower limit.
